east grinstead.s1_head: Charity and volunteer work in East Grinstead
s1loc: East Grinstead has a busy local charity scene. East Grinstead Foodbank, a Trussell network member, runs from Jubilee Community Centre on Charlwoods Road and depends on the town for food donations, volunteers and funds, with collection points at churches and surgeries. The big food-redistribution and foodbank networks keep parcels moving alongside it, and St Catherine's Hospice has opened a smart new shop at Whitehall Parade on London Road, selling clothing, books and refurbished bikes restored with Recycle Your Cycle to fund its palliative care.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities hold high-street shops and central buying accounts, from St Catherine's Hospice retail to the larger fundraising names, while small community groups, pantries and volunteer-run foodbanks work on a shoestring across Imberhorne, Felbridge and Ashurst Wood. East Grinstead Foodbank fields a team of volunteers sorting, packing and signposting through its crisis line. We are set up to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts and direct online ordering, no minimum.

Beyond the food parcels, East Grinstead carries a wider voluntary layer. St Catherine's Hospice, which serves Crawley, Horsham, Mid Sussex and South East Surrey, runs charity shops and a furniture operation funded by hundreds of retail volunteers. Catherine's Bridal sits within the new London Road store, and the town's many independent charity shops add a strong retail presence. Local churches, mutual-aid groups and the volunteer drivers around Lingfield and Forest Row form a network of small projects distinct from the foodbank itself.

didcot.s1_head: Charity and volunteer work in Didcot
s1loc: Didcot sits at the centre of Oxfordshire food support. Didcot Foodbank, a project of Didcot Baptist Church on Wantage Road, hands out emergency parcels through a voucher referral system, while SOFEA runs Didcot Community Larder at the Northbourne Centre, a pop-up hub for surplus food, friendship and savings on bills. FareShare Thames Valley is based right here in Didcot, redistributing surplus food to South Oxfordshire charities and community groups and offering warehouse training and volunteering placements.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities keep high-street shops and central buying accounts, including Helen and Douglas House with its furniture store on Broadway, while small community groups, pantries and volunteer-run foodbanks work on a shoestring across Ladygrove, Northbourne and Great Western Park. SOFEA and the Baptist Church foodbank lean on local volunteers for morning set-up, packing and running larder sessions. We are set up to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts and direct online ordering, no minimum.

Didcot's voluntary scene reaches wider still. Helen and Douglas House runs its children's hospice furniture and general store on Broadway, raising funds through pre-loved clothing, toys and bric-a-brac. SOFEA, a social enterprise based in Didcot, redistributes food across the Thames Valley and trains young people into work, while Oxfordshire's volunteer network signs residents up to larder and foodbank roles. These hospice shops, community larders and volunteer-run projects across Ladygrove and Great Western Park sit distinct from the emergency foodbank itself.

melton mowbray.s1_head: Charity and volunteer work in Melton Mowbray
s1loc: Melton Mowbray has a strong community food network. Leicester South Foodbank runs centres serving the area, including at The Old School on Grantham Road in nearby Bottesford and Bradgate Flats in Asfordby, drawing on volunteers to sort and signpost. FareShare Midlands, working from warehouses in Birmingham, Leicester and Nottingham, redistributes surplus food to more than 650 charity and community-group members across the region, much of it donated by local Tesco stores through the wider food-redistribution networks.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities keep high-street shops and central buying accounts, from LOROS Hospice retail to Rainbows children's hospice with its Sherrard Street shop, while small community groups, pantries and volunteer-run foodbanks work on a shoestring across the Vale of Belvoir, Asfordby and Bottesford. FareShare Midlands relies on volunteers to drive vans, sort food in warehouses and run distribution. We are set up to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts and direct online ordering, no minimum.

Melton's voluntary layer runs wider still. LOROS Hospice cares for thousands across Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland and is planning a community hub in the town, funded through its charity shops. Rainbows Hospice runs its Sherrard Street store, and Dove Cottage Day Hospice keeps shops across the Vale of Belvoir villages of Bottesford, Stathern and Asfordby. The borough council's volunteering scheme and Voluntary Action Leicestershire link residents to bereavement support and small projects distinct from the foodbanks themselves.

clydebank.s1_head: Charity and volunteer work in Clydebank
s1loc: Clydebank has a deep-rooted community sector. West Dunbartonshire Community Foodshare delivers emergency food parcels across the area, from fresh and frozen to toiletries, baby items and pet food, open weekdays with a freephone line. Food for Thought runs from the Artizan Shopping Centre weekday mornings, and Cosy Afternoons offers free homemade soup and company at Centre 81 in Whitecrook on Fridays. The big food-redistribution networks keep these pantries and warm spaces stocked across the town.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities keep high-street shops and central buying accounts, including St Margaret of Scotland Hospice with its volunteer-run shops at Clyde Shopping Centre, while small community groups, pantries and volunteer-run foodbanks work on a shoestring across Whitecrook, Drumry and Old Kilpatrick. Old Kilpatrick Food Parcels and the Tontine Food Pantry at Renton lean wholly on local volunteers. We are set up to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts and direct online ordering, no minimum.

Clydebank's voluntary layer runs wider still. St Margaret of Scotland Hospice, the first and largest hospice in Scotland, has cared for patients since 1950 and receives over 14,000 volunteer hours a year, funding that work through its Clyde Shopping Centre shops. Churches and community groups run regular food pantries and warm spaces with free tea and coffee across Whitecrook and Drumry, and the area's volunteer centres match residents to soup-kitchen and parcel roles. These hospice shops, pantries and mutual-aid groups sit distinct from the foodbank itself.

daventry.s1_head: Charity and volunteer work in Daventry
s1loc: Daventry has a long-standing grassroots charity scene. Daventry Food Bank, set up and run by Vineyard Community Church since 2010, has supported thousands of families through emergency food, working with over 400 referring agencies including Citizens Advice, the council, schools and surgeries. It sits within Food Aid Alliance West Northants, a group of food banks, community larders and social supermarkets, all of which lean heavily on volunteers, alongside the wider food-redistribution networks supplying the district.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities keep high-street shops and central buying accounts, from hospice retailers to the larger fundraising names, while small community groups, pantries and volunteer-run foodbanks work on a shoestring across Southbrook, Middlemore and the surrounding villages. Daventry Food Bank's amazing team of volunteers collects, sorts and packs parcels, greets recipients and offers a listening ear. We are set up to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts and direct online ordering, no minimum.

Daventry's voluntary layer runs wider still. Cynthia Spencer Hospice teams work within Danetre Hospital in the town, with the hospice funding its palliative care through warehouse-style charity shops selling furniture, clothing and books across Northamptonshire. Age UK runs a Daventry shop of quality second-hand clothing, and Volunteer Centre Daventry has been at the heart of district volunteering since 1990, matching residents to foodbank, larder and community roles distinct from the foodbank itself.

thatcham.s1_head: Charity and volunteer work in Thatcham
s1loc: Thatcham shares a busy charity landscape with neighbouring Newbury. West Berks Foodbank, formerly the Newbury and Thatcham Food Bank, runs a Thursday session at Greenham Business Park serving Thatcham through a voucher referral system, part of a weekly rota that also covers Calcot, Newbury, Hungerford and Burghfield. The foodbank relies on the local community for donations, volunteering and funds, with a Thatcham charity recently donating slow cookers, while the big food-redistribution networks keep parcels and meals flowing across the district.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities keep high-street shops and central buying accounts, from hospice retailers to the larger fundraising names, while small community groups, pantries and volunteer-run foodbanks work on a shoestring across Henwick, Colthrop and Cold Ash. West Berks Foodbank's volunteers, like lead volunteer Sue Harrison who started during lockdown, are central to packing and signposting. We are set up to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts and direct online ordering, no minimum.

Thatcham's voluntary layer runs wider still. West Berkshire's voluntary sector, listed by the council, knits together charity shops, community groups and volunteer-run projects across the town and surrounding parishes. Local churches host the foodbank sessions, residents fundraise street by street for parcels, and neighbourhood schemes around Henwick and Cold Ash recruit drivers and helpers. These charity shops, community projects and mutual-aid groups across Thatcham sit distinct from the foodbank centres themselves, knitting together a network that runs on volunteer goodwill.

kingswinford.s1_head: Charity and volunteer work in Kingswinford
s1loc: Kingswinford sits within Dudley's strong voluntary sector. Black Country Foodbank helps families in crisis with three days of emergency food while longer-term support is arranged, running a Kingswinford centre at Our Lady of Lourdes Catholic Church on Summerhill from its central warehouse in Brierley Hill. The Giving Hands Charity works from The Warehouse on Cottage Street and The Brierley Hill Project on South Street, while the big food-redistribution networks keep parcels and toiletries moving to households across the area.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities keep high-street shops and central buying accounts, from hospice retailers to the larger fundraising names, while small community groups, pantries and volunteer-run foodbanks work on a shoestring across Wall Heath, Pensnett and Wordsley. Black Country Foodbank and the Giving Hands Charity lean wholly on local volunteers to sort, pack and distribute. We are set up to serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts and direct online ordering, no minimum.

Kingswinford's voluntary layer runs wider still. Brierley Hill Babybank, which works to relieve poverty across Brierley Hill and the surrounding area, runs volunteering opportunities in Kingswinford itself. Dudley CVS Volunteer Centre, based on Albion Street in Brierley Hill, advises and matches potential volunteers to local organisations recruiting, and Mary Stevens Hospice funds free care through charity shops across the borough. These hospice shops, baby banks and mutual-aid groups around Wall Heath and Wordsley sit distinct from the foodbank centres themselves.
